117610.name: Lubavitch Chabad of Illinois
117610.note: CrownHeights.info (6 June 2007, from COL): 'Over the past thirty years Lubavitch Chabad of Illinois has grown from a one-man operation in a small Chicago apartment to a legion of more than thirty institutions'; Rabbi Daniel Moscowitz was cheered 'for his thirty years on the job'. Lubavitch.com (4 March 2014, his obituary): 'The Chicago-born rabbi led the city's Chabad community since 1977.' Medium: Chabad.org (on CrownHeights.info, 12 July 2022) says that in 1975 the Rebbe 'sent Rabbi Daniel and Esther Rochel Moscowitz to Chicago to increase Chabad activities in the city'. Before them: in 1942 'the Sixth Rebbe dispatched Rabbi Shlomo Zalman (Solomon S.) and Chaya Sora Hecht to the city' (the same article), to Congregation Anshei Lubavitch (founded 1875); Rabbi Hecht was 'the Head Shliach of the state' until his passing (JUF News, 5 March 2014), and then Moscowitz 'took over as regional director of Lubavitch Chabad of Illinois' (Chabad.org on COLlive, 21 Nov 2019). Now 2825 W Howard Street; a three-story headquarters modeled on 770 broke ground in April 2022.

earlier.where: a small Chicago apartment (a one-man operation)

118199.name: Congregation B'nei Ruven
118199.note: An old Chicago congregation led by the Rebbe's shluchim since 1958. Lubavitch.com (April 2010, Mrs. Chava Devorah Shusterman's obituary): 'In 1947, the sixth Rebbe instructed the Shustermans to move to Chicago', first to the Agudas Chabad synagogue in Uptown-Edgewater; 'In 1958, the Bnei Reuven synagogue, one of the oldest congregations in Chicago, invited Rabbi Shusterman to serve as its rabbi.' The new building was a long project ('the synagogue was finally built'; in 1969 it 'was awarded a prize for its unique architectural design'). Chabad.org (on CrownHeights.info, 12 July 2022): B'nei Ruven 'eventually became the city's largest Orthodox congregation'; 'Rabbi Shusterman, who was joined at B'nei Ruven by Rabbi Baruch and Chanie Hertz in 1990, led B'nei Ruven as senior rabbi until his passing in 2001.' Medium: the congregation itself is older (its founding year not found) and the 2022 article lists it among Chicago's Chabad congregations from before the shluchim. Now 6350 N Whipple Street.

117612.name: F.R.E.E.
117612.note: Chabad.org (on CrownHeights.info, 4 Dec 2020, Reitza Kosofsky's obituary): she 'was the longtime president of F.R.E.E. (Friends of Refugees of Eastern Europe) of Chicago and an indefatigable pioneer of outreach in the Russian-Jewish community since 1973. From its humble beginnings in the Kosofsky home, F.R.E.E has since grown into a major landmark'. Chabad.org (12 July 2022): 'In the early 1970s, as Jews began streaming out of the Soviet Union, Reitza Kosofsky began organizing social, religious and humanitarian programming for them.' Medium: 1973 is the start of her outreach; when it took the name F.R.E.E. is not stated. Rabbi Shmuel Notik directed F.R.E.E. of Illinois (CrownHeights.info, 2006); Rabbi Levi Notik now; 2935 W. Devon Avenue.

Hecht and Rabbi Daniel Moscowitz.' Medium: JUF News (2 Dec 2016) says a new appointment 'coincides with the 40th anniversary of the opening of the first Chabad House in Illinois' (so 1976). The Daily Northwestern (1 Oct 2005): 'When Rabbi Dov Hillel Klein moved to Evanston 20 years ago to serve Northwestern's Tannenbaum Chabad House'.
